content.thinking:
I'm checking how the texture parameter works on the part builder and decal types, then sketching out the module structure with a vector helper and a seeded RNG for building the elven archer model.

Now I'm working out the skeleton: hip joint, spine chain rising through spine1/spine2/chest with specific coordinates, then a neck chain parented to the chest leading up to a head joint tilted slightly forward. I'm also planning the torso loft stations from hips to shoulders, narrowing at the waist and widening at the chest for an anime-style silhouette, ending with a rounded cap near the shoulder line.

I'm deciding on a cream stand-up collar ring with gold trim at the neckline rather than a V-neck, and confirming the torso mesh binds to the hips and spine chain with the lower torso attached to the hip joint. Next I'm starting on the pelvis and leg structure, with pants draped over the hips.

Now I'm working out tunic skirt panels hanging from the belt at the front and back with a leaf-dagged, gold-trimmed hem, making sure the panel width and extrusion keep it flaring outside the thigh radius at hip height.

I decide to split the front into two asymmetric half-panels (left and right, like an open slit skirt) with zigzag hems, tilting each outward slightly for a dynamic archer-style drape rather than a flat symmetric skirt.

For the back, I'm keeping a single long panel with a concave hem that tucks under the cape, and I'm starting to define the belt loop sweep around the hips.

Actually, the sweep orientation around a closed loop is ambiguous, so I'll switch strategies and build the belt as a simple lathe ring around the torso instead, using a small rectangular profile revolved around the vertical axis.

For the pauldron I'll use dome-shaped lathes tilted outward over the shoulder, with smaller layered domes cascading down the arm like lames. I'm painting gold rim trim where the lathe height is near the base, plus faint radial vein lines across the dome surface by checking angle modulo patterns.

For hair, instead of separate caps I'm thinking of lofting a helmet-like shell over the skull from crown to hairline, offset slightly outward and shifted back, though I need to watch that the front ellipse doesn't swallow the face.

That bottom edge forms a clean straight hairline, with fringe locks adding jagged coverage on top. For the back and sides, I'll use a second partial ellipsoid excluding the front arc, dropping down to around ear level, then add a separate back hair mass with flowing strands — maybe a high ponytail or braid as a jointed chain running from the back of the head down to the waist.

I'll make that braid thick with segment bands for texture, plus two long swept side locks framing the face down to the chest, 7-9 pointed bangs locks fanning across the forehead, and 5 big pointed locks fanning down the back (the cape covers the left side so it's fine to skip that area). For color, I'm leaning toward a cel-shaded silver base with a subtle vertical gradient toward lavender at the tips, maybe with a highlight band for the lit side.

Now I'm thinking about a gold elven circlet swept as a closed ring around the forehead with a glowing emerald gem at front. The issue is the ring's height would fall right where the hair cap's bottom edge sits, so it'd get hidden under the hair -- I need to lift the circlet's placement higher so it sits visibly above the hairline instead of being swallowed by it.

That gives roughly 7.4 heads tall, which reads as an elegant anime-leaning proportion. Checking eye placement against the head midpoint, placing eyes slightly below center at 1.715 versus midpoint 1.72 fits the typical lower-eye anime convention.

Now I'm plotting out the facial feature positions more precisely: eyes around y=1.69, nose at 1.655, mouth at 1.628, chin at 1.595, with mouth sitting right at the jaw seam. Then I'm working through loft stations for the head profile, defining center depth, width, and height at each vertical slice from the crown down through the cheekbones to capture the rounded cap shape and widest point near 1.70.

Continuing the loft stations down into the jaw and chin region, I'm computing where the head mesh ends and the jaw mesh begins, tracking forward-depth values to check the chin doesn't recede too much — comparing front-z at chin versus forehead versus eyes to make sure the chin reads as small and pointed rather than receding, which fits the anime-style look I'm going for. Now I'm thinking through the catmull-rom loft orientation, figuring out how width and height axes should align as the path curves downward.

Each loft segment gets its own bone for rigid skinning — head bone drives the head loft, jaw bone drives the jaw loft — with the end caps left round since they're hidden inside adjacent geometry. I'm placing the ears, then moving on to define the neck as a tapering sweep along the neck bone chain with skin-colored shading, and starting to set up the arm sweep from the shoulder through elbow to wrist.

Now for the arm sleeves I'm deciding on the color blocking: upper arm in an emerald tunic sleeve down to about the elbow with a gold cuff ring, then a cream undershirt sleeve peeking out, followed by a leather ranger's bracer with gold trim on the forearm, with skin showing elsewhere.

I'm calculating the exact t-values for each band based on actual segment lengths so the elbow and bracer boundaries line up correctly, then adding gold edge rings and crossed lacing detail to the bracer for texture.

Now I'm moving to the legs, setting up the hip joint positions and a chain that sweeps from hip through knee to ankle, adjusting the thigh radius along the way.

Adding the boot cuff ring...

Now thinking through boot decorations: gold trim at the cuff and a laced pattern on the front of the shin, using surface normal and position checks to paint small alternating gold bars along the lacing line.

For the sole I'm considering a sector-based darker shading band around the foot bottom, and deciding knee guards aren't needed since the pants cuff covers that detail.

Next I'll move to ears, facial details, and the hairpiece, then add glowing gems at the circlet, pauldron, bow, and cape clasp.

For equipment I'm positioning a hip-slung dagger sheath angled down-back with the hilt up, plus a belt pouch and a quiver baldric strap running diagonally from the back over the shoulder to the opposite hip.

Since the strap mostly hides under the cape at the back, I don't need to worry too much about exact visibility there. For the strap's cross-section, I'm thinking a flattened sweep shape so it lies naturally against the body, but orienting the sweep's roll so it stays flat against the torso surface is tricky without being able to specify the normal explicitly.

I'll just test with initial normals and preview the result, adjusting if it looks twisted. If the flat strap doesn't orient correctly, I could try a rounded tube or an elliptical cross-section instead, but I'll start simple and check. I'm also setting the cape to have subtle drift rather than static rigidity, even in rest pose.

Now defining the cape's shape, starting with its top and hem curves as catmull-rom splines through several 3D control points.

For the membrane paint logic, I'm separating outer and inner faces by normal direction — teal on the outward-facing side (back), cream lining on the inward-facing side toward the body — and considering a gold band near the hem edge. To make the hem feel more dynamic, I'm adding extra waypoints with a zigzag pattern in y and z so the edge reads as dagged and flowing rather than straight.

Now I'm thinking the sawtooth dag points won't align well with evenly-spaced membrane columns since the hem gets resampled by arc length, so I should bump the column count up (like 40) to preserve those sharp points, plus push the hem outward and down in z to get that classic cape billow look. I'm also considering adding a leaf-shaped gold gorget around the neck as a clasp detail, tying into how the cape attaches at the shoulder via a pauldron.

Moving on to the hands, I'm writing a helper to orthogonalize direction vectors, then building out the palm and finger geometry using frustum-shaped boxes swept along the wrist-to-fingertip direction, with an "up" vector controlling the roll orientation of each segment.

Writing finger spacing and chain logic...

Skipping tiny nail details for now. For the thumb, I'm positioning its base offset from the wrist with an outward rotation toward the fist direction and palm normal, then defining two segments with specific lengths and curl angles for a clenched pose.

For the left fist, I'm thinking through where the palm normal points and how the curl angles increase along the finger joints, then working out the grip point on the bow by offsetting from the knuckle row position along the palm normal and wrist direction, treating the vertical axis as orthogonal to the thumb direction.

Checking the forearm orientation against the grip direction, the bend angle seems too large to look natural for a bow-at-side pose, so I'm reconsidering the elbow height to get a more believable arm angle.

Placing the bow grip near the left hip with the bow curving in front of the body, I'm giving the right arm a more extended, open pose for symmetry — left arm bent to hold the bow, right arm reaching out roughly 40° from the body with a relaxed hand, keeping the overall pose readable for rigging while still accommodating the prop.

Continuing the right arm chain to the wrist, then setting the hand position and palm normal facing forward-in, with fingers slightly curled and the thumb extended outward.

For the right hand with palm facing forward, the thumb points laterally outward away from the body. For the left hand making a fist with palm facing inward toward the body midline, the thumb points upward.

Now I'm working out the bow's orientation: it's vertical in the YZ plane at the grip's x-position, with the grip riser running along y and wrapped in leather with gold accent rings. The fingers wrap around the grip from the back side, curling in the plane defined by the draw direction and the negative-x axis, and the bow's recurve tips angle toward the archer with the belly facing forward. The legs stand slightly apart with toes turned outward, and now I'm considering the facial expression.

Eyebrows get folded into the eye decal. For hair, I'm designing a reusable lock-building function that sweeps a tapered, flattened tube along a curved path, with width functions controlling the ribbon-like cross-section so it reads as flat strands rather than round tubes -- orienting the flat face outward for side locks, and setting up a horizontal sweep direction for bangs crossing the forehead.

I'll define bangs as root-to-tip paths curving from the hairline down and sideways, parameterized by root/tip x-positions and lean, using around seven roughly symmetrical locks. Cap shading will use the same cel-shaded lighting model for consistency, and I'm now planning the back hair as a ponytail/braid chain attached at a hair tie point behind the head.

For the braid path, I realize it would intersect the cape geometry if hung straight down the back, so I'm shifting it to drape over the right shoulder instead, falling down the front of the chest where it stays visible and avoids the collision.

That radius keeps it tucked inside the covering even near the shoulder. I'm treating the braid as a chain of joints parented to the head, running down the chest despite being a bit unusual rigging, functioning essentially as a tail.

Now I'm worried the quiver strap over the right shoulder will collide with the braid's position, so I'm considering shifting the braid to the left shoulder near the pauldron and cape, or routing it down the center-right of the back instead to avoid the conflict.

So the back arrangement settles into quiver on the right, braid in the center, cape on the left, with the braid hanging close against the back torso. I'm working out the cape's exact outline, keeping it narrower at the top and flared at the hem, while placing the quiver and braid at specific depths behind the torso so they don't visually overlap.

Now for the chest I'm adding detail: a diagonal strap, a gold filigree vine at center, and a V-neck opening revealing the cream undershirt beneath, defined by a region where the surface faces forward and sits above a certain height. I'm also tracing a thin gold line along the edge of that V-neck opening to give it a finished, laced look.

For the full tunic paint function, I'm layering a base green cel-shaded color with the cream V-neck inset, considering a darker side panel lower on the torso, and thinking about whether to add a lighter trim near the waist or keep it simple — using nested cel-shading helpers so both the fabric and the gold trim get consistent toon shading.

I'm also weighing whether to add vine-pattern decals on the chest, but the diagonal strap crossing the torso conflicts with that placement, so I'm considering moving the strap's path instead and working out the exact shoulder-to-hip coordinates for it.

Writing SVG vine motif code...

For the feather fletch card, I'll tint only greyscale textures and keep a colored teal-and-white SVG as is. Now I'm writing the TypeScript file carefully, defining vector helper types and checking where the Joint type should be imported from in the skeleton module.

input.command: grep -n "^export" src/builder.ts src/skeleton.ts src/frame.ts src/index.ts | head -60; cat scripts/preview.ts 2>/dev/null | head -5; cat package.json | head -30
